questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the economy of your Country, what will be the nature of price elasticity of demand in relation to the following goods?

(i) Electricity. (2 marks)
(ii) Biscuit. (2 marks)
(iii) Pipe borne water. (2 marks)
(iv) Salt. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how much the quantity demanded responds to a change in price. Demand is **inelastic** when PED is less than 1 (quantity changes proportionately less than price) and **elastic** when PED is greater than 1. For an economy like Cameroon's, the nature of demand is as follows.

| Good | Nature of price elasticity of demand | Main reason |
|---|---|---|
| (i) Electricity | **Inelastic** (PED < 1) | A necessity for lighting, cooking and running machines, with no cheap close substitute in the short run |
| (ii) Biscuit | **Elastic** (PED > 1) | Not a necessity; many substitutes (bread, groundnuts, fruit, local snacks) |
| (iii) Pipe borne water | **Inelastic** (PED < 1) | A basic need of life; few substitutes for most households |
| (iv) Salt | **Highly (almost perfectly) inelastic** (PED close to 0) | A necessity, very cheap, bought in tiny quantities, a negligible part of income, no substitute |

**Explanation.**

- **Electricity:** households and firms need it every day; a rise in price makes them economise a little, but the quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises.
- **Biscuit:** if its price rises, consumers easily switch to cheaper snacks or go without, so the quantity demanded falls by a larger percentage than the price rise.
- **Pipe borne water:** people must drink, cook and wash; the only alternatives (wells, streams) are less convenient or not available everywhere, so the quantity demanded hardly changes when the price changes.
- **Salt:** a change in its price is so small relative to income that consumers do not change the amount they buy.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State the corresponding words to the following:

(i) Price set below the equilibrium price. (2 marks)
(ii) Price set above the equilibrium price. (2 marks)
(iii) A condition in which quantity demanded is equal to quantity supplied. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Price set below the equilibrium price.** When the authorities fix a price below equilibrium it is a **maximum price (price ceiling)**. At that price the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied, so there is **excess demand (a shortage)**.

**(ii) Price set above the equilibrium price.** When a price is fixed above equilibrium it is a **minimum price (price floor)**. At that price the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded, so there is **excess supply (a surplus)**.

**(iii) Quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.** This is **market equilibrium**: the price at which it occurs is the **equilibrium (market-clearing) price**, and the quantity traded is the equilibrium quantity. There is neither a shortage nor a surplus, so there is no pressure on the price to change.

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain THREE (3) uses of price elasticity of demand to the producer (businessman). (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The price elasticity of demand (PED) tells a producer how sensitive buyers are to a change in price. It is useful in the following ways.

1. **Pricing decisions and total revenue.** Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold. Suppose (hypothetical figures) a firm sells 1,000 units at 500 FCFA, so revenue is $500\times1\,000=500\,000$ FCFA. If demand is **elastic** and the firm raises the price to 600 FCFA, sales may fall to 700 units and revenue falls to $600\times700=420\,000$ FCFA; the firm should rather *lower* the price. If demand is **inelastic**, the same price rise may only reduce sales to 950 units and revenue rises to $600\times950=570\,000$ FCFA; the firm should *raise* the price.
2. **Price discrimination.** If the producer sells in two markets with different elasticities (for example local buyers and foreign buyers, or peak and off-peak times), he can charge a higher price where demand is inelastic and a lower price where it is elastic, and so increase total revenue.
3. **Passing on costs and taxes to consumers.** When the cost of production or a tax rises, the producer can raise the price and shift most of the burden to buyers if demand is inelastic; if demand is elastic he must absorb most of the rise or he will lose sales.

**Conclusion.** Knowledge of elasticity helps the businessman to choose the price that maximises revenue and profit and to forecast the effect of changes in price, cost or tax.
